summary: Today's strongest signal is health-data lock-in: Withings now charges new users $99/year just to sync with Apple Health, and people are still hand-exporting Garmin and MacroFactor data into spreadsheets. Smaller themes are the fear of an Apple ID lockout cutting off banking apps and daily life, and Meetup's decline for hobby groups. Note: Reddit, X, Bluesky and Stack Exchange were blocked from this environment, so all evidence today comes from Hacker News and only well-supported ideas are listed.

ideas.title: OpenSync: free health-data bridge between scales, watches and Apple Health / Health Connect
ideas.oneLiner: A phone app that pulls data from Withings, Garmin and similar devices and writes it into Apple Health or Health Connect, plus a one-tap CSV export, with no subscription.
ideas.problem: Device makers are paywalling or restricting access to the user's own health data. Withings now requires $99/year for new users to sync with Apple Health, Garmin's developer access and account export are slow, and users resort to weekly manual exports into spreadsheets or typing weights into Health by hand.
ideas.targetUsers: People with smart scales, blood pressure cuffs, watches and glucose monitors who want all their data in one place (Apple Health, Health Connect, or their own spreadsheet), especially quantified-self and chronic-condition users.
ideas.monetization: One-time purchase (around ₹799 / $9.99) or a small yearly fee for automatic background sync of multiple vendors; free manual CSV export.
mvp: Connect a Withings account via the user's own login/API token and import weight, body fat and blood pressure
Write imported readings into Apple Health (Flutter health plugin) and Health Connect on Android
Import Garmin full-account export files (FIT/CSV) so users do not wait days for the next one
Weekly one-tap CSV/Sheets export of weight, sleep, nutrition and activity in a single tidy table
Local-only storage, no account required on our side

competitors.name: Health Sync (Android)
competitors.gap: Subscription-based and mostly focused on Fitbit/Garmin to Google Fit/Health Connect. Does not solve the Withings to Apple Health paywall.

competitors.name: Syncfit (Fitbit to Apple Health)
competitors.gap: Focused on Fitbit with its own $9.99/month or $39.99/year tiers, so it does not cover Withings or a cross-vendor spreadsheet export.

competitors.name: Apple Health / Withings support workaround
competitors.gap: Withings' own suggestion is a manual refresh because of iOS limits, and syncing is not automatic, which is the pain users describe.

ideas.title: Cold Standby: a lockout survival kit for your Apple or Google account
ideas.oneLiner: An app that maps which banking, payment, ID and subscription apps depend on your Apple/Google account and keeps an offline, encrypted lifeboat so a lockout does not stop daily life.
ideas.problem: A locked Apple ID can brick the App Store, which in turn stops banking and payment apps from launching when they force version updates. There is no human escalation path, and recovery can take days or leave devices and accessories permanently tied to the old account.
ideas.targetUsers: Heavy single-ecosystem Apple or Google users, expats, and anyone whose payments and IDs live on one phone.
ideas.monetization: Free checklist and inventory; paid tier (around ₹299/month or $2.99/month) for encrypted offline export bundle, reminders to re-verify recovery contacts, and family sharing.
mvp: Guided inventory of critical apps (banking, payments, government ID, 2FA) and which account each depends on
Checklist to set up recovery contacts, legacy contacts and a second device or secondary phone with the critical apps pre-installed
Encrypted offline export of the inventory plus recovery codes (printable PDF)
Quarterly reminders to re-test the backup plan
Short playbook for the first 24 hours of a lockout

competitors.name: Apple recovery and legacy contacts
competitors.gap: Only works with other Apple users, and does not cover the dependent app ecosystem (banking apps that force updates) during a lockout.

competitors.name: Bitwarden Emergency Access
competitors.gap: Protects vault access but does not model which services depend on which platform account or how to keep payments working during a lockout.

ideas.title: TableCrew: a lightweight Meetup replacement for recurring hobby groups
ideas.oneLiner: A simple, cheap scheduling and RSVP page for recurring game nights, run clubs and hobby groups that does not push organizers onto Meetup's fees.
ideas.problem: Organizers describe Meetup as having declined with every change, but stay because Discord and Facebook feel worse and members are used to it. Recurring hobby groups lose members when scheduling and RSVPs are clumsy.
ideas.targetUsers: Organizers of recurring local groups such as board games, tabletop RPGs, running, book clubs and language exchanges.
ideas.monetization: Free for small groups; flat organizer plan (around ₹499/month or $5/month) for larger groups, reminders and recurring events. No per-member fees.
mvp: Public group page with recurring events and one-tap RSVP (no member account required)
Email and WhatsApp-share reminders before each session
Waitlist and venue capacity limits
Simple 'who's bringing what' list for each session
Import existing member list from CSV

competitors.name: Meetup
competitors.gap: Organizer fees keep rising and users call the experience enshittified.

competitors.name: Heylo
competitors.gap: Aimed at clubs and hobby groups, but its pricing and transaction fees mean it is not the free, minimal option organizers want.

competitors.name: Mobilizon
competitors.gap: Free and open source but requires running your own server.

ideas.title: Passkey Map: see which logins use passkeys, who shares them, and how to recover
ideas.oneLiner: A browser extension that tracks which of your accounts use passkeys versus passwords, flags shared-household logins, and keeps recovery notes.
ideas.problem: Passkeys behave inconsistently across sites: some require both passkey and password, some use separate passkeys per regional domain, and it becomes hard to share a login with a spouse. Users end up confused about what protects which account.
ideas.targetUsers: Families and small households sharing accounts (accounting tools, shopping, streaming) who are mid-migration to passkeys.
ideas.monetization: Free for up to 20 accounts; around $2/month for household sharing and recovery notes.
mvp: Detect passkey vs password vs both on login pages and log it locally
Per-account note: who in the household needs access and how it is shared
Warn when an account is passkey-only with no recovery method recorded
Group regional domains (for example Amazon .com/.co.uk/.de) under one entry
Encrypted local export

competitors.name: Bitwarden / 1Password
competitors.gap: Store passkeys and support family sharing, but users still report regional-domain duplicates and password-plus-passkey flows they cannot share, and neither gives a clear per-account map of recovery status. Weakest differentiation of today's ideas.

sources.title: Passkeys are not a trap
sources.quote: Now when I login, I'm required to give both the passkey from my password manager and usually my password, too. It's a usability mess and basically makes it impossible for me to share my login with e.g. my wife when she might need to login to that account.

sources.title: Passkeys are not a trap
sources.quote: Amazon.com, UK, DE, JP, all need different passkeys. Yet my password and TOTP works across them all seamlessly.
